name: Booby Cay

name: Staniel Rock
note: Staniel: the old word for a kestrel, as in Staniel Cay in the Exumas

name: Petrel Holm
note: Petrels wail at night from their burrows

name: Isle of Devils
note: Spanish sailors' name for Bermuda, after the night shrieks of its nesting petrels

name: Shrieking Isle
note: Seabirds calling in the dark, taken for spirits

name: Laughing Gull Cay
note: After Belize's Laughing Bird Caye, named for the gulls that bred there

name: Gannet Stack
note: A stack whitened by nesting gannets

name: Solan Stack
note: Solan goose: the old seamen's name for the gannet

name: Grog-Grog Rock
note: Smyth's Sailor's Word-Book (1867): grog-grog, the soft cry of the solan goose

name: Shag Rock
note: Shags, the sea cormorants, dry their wings on it

name: Mother Carey's Rock
note: Storm petrels, 'Mother Carey's chickens', were said to foretell a gale

name: Albatross Rock
note: Albatrosses were thought to carry the souls of drowned sailors

name: Pelican Cay
note: A cay name wherever pelicans fish

name: Man-o'-War Cay
note: Man-o'-war bird: the sailors' name for the frigatebird

name: Frigatebird Island
note: Frigatebirds roost in its trees, red throats puffed

name: Curlew Holm
note: Cook named a Curlew Island in Dusky Sound, 1773

name: Puffin Holm
note: A grassy holm riddled with puffin burrows

name: Tern Cay
note: Terns nest on the bare sand

name: Noddy Cay
note: Noddies: tropical terns so tame that sailors thought them foolish

name: Parrot Cay
note: After the Parrot Cays of Abaco, home of the Bahama parrot

name: Pigeon Cay
note: One of the commonest names on Bahamian charts

name: Egg Island
note: Sailors landed to gather seabird and turtle eggs; Eleuthera has one

name: Hummingbird Cay
note: As in the Exuma Cays

name: Raven Rock
note: A black rock where ravens sit

name: Hawksbill Cay
note: After the hawksbill turtle, whose shell was the period's tortoiseshell

name: Turtle Cay
note: Green turtles come ashore to lay; Bahamian cays were named for them

name: Loggerhead Key
note: Loggerhead turtles nest here; Key is the older spelling of cay

name: Sea Wolf Rocks
note: Spanish sailors called the Caribbean monk seal the sea wolf, hence Cay Lobos

name: Seal Holm
note: Seals haul out on its ledges

name: Selkie Skerry
note: Orkney selkies: seals that shed their skins and walk ashore as people

name: Whaleback Island
note: A long, low ridge like a whale's back breaking the surface

name: Grampus Rock
note: Grampus: the old seamen's name for a blowing, spouting whale

name: Porpoise Isle
note: Porpoises play in its tide race

name: Crab Cay
note: Land crabs swarm its scrub at night

name: Conch Cay
note: Conch shells heaped on the beach

name: Barracuda Cay
note: Barracuda hang over its reef

name: Bonefish Cay
note: Bonefish tail on the flats around it

name: Snapper Cay
note: Good fishing for snapper off its edge

name: Nurse Cay
note: Nurse sharks sleep in its shallows; as in the Ragged Island Range

name: Oyster Cay
note: Mangrove oysters grow on its roots

name: Crawfish Cay
note: Crawfish: the Caribbean spiny lobster

name: Mermaid's Purse Cay
note: Mermaid's purse: the empty egg case of a skate, found on the tide line

name: Devilfish Rock
note: Devil-fish: the anglerfish, 'a hideous creature' (Smyth)

name: Inkfish Rock
note: Inkfish: the period name for squid and cuttlefish

name: Flying Fish Cay
note: Flying fish land on deck at night in these waters

name: Sea Cow Island
note: Sea cow: the sailors' name for the manatee grazing its seagrass

name: Seahorse Cay
note: Seahorses cling to its seagrass

name: Grey Amber Cay
note: Ambergris, 'grey amber', washed up from whales and was worth its weight in gold

name: Whalebone Cay
note: A whale's ribs bleach on its beach

name: Sea Grape Cay
note: Sea grape grows on sandy shores; its fruit makes a jam

name: Coco Plum Cay
note: Coco plum: a beach shrub with sweet fruit

name: Mangrove Cay
note: Mangroves standing in the water on their roots

name: Lignum Vitae Cay
note: Lignum vitae, ironwood: so dense it sinks; turned into sheaves for blocks

name: Pumpion Cay
note: Pumpion: the old word for pumpkin, kept on a cay off Andros

name: Calabash Cay
note: Calabash gourds served sailors as bowls and bailers

name: Manchineel Cay

name: Poisonwood Cay
note: Poisonwood: brush against it and blister

name: Samphire Rock
note: Rock samphire, gathered from sea cliffs and pickled: 'half way down hangs one that gathers samphire' (King Lear)

name: Thrift Holm
note: Thrift, the sea pink, carpets its turf

name: Garlic Holm
note: After Ganinick in Scilly, Cornish for the place of wild garlic

name: Elder Isle
note: Tresco in Scilly is Cornish for the farm by the elder trees

name: Scurvy Grass Holm
note: Scurvy grass: the bitter cress sailors ate against scurvy

name: Tamarind Isle
note: Tamarind pods against scurvy and thirst

name: Breadfruit Island
note: The Bounty was carrying breadfruit plants when her crew mutinied

name: Nutmeg Isle
note: Spice islands were the richest landfall of the age

name: Cinnamon Cay
note: Cinnamon bark drying in the sun

name: Clove Isle
note: Cloves: once worth more than their weight in silver

name: Pepper Cay
note: Pepper grows wild in its thickets

name: Ginger Cay
note: As in the Bahamas' Ginger Cay

name: Lime Cay
note: Limes against scurvy; there is one off Port Royal in Jamaica

name: Wild Orange Cay
note: Sour oranges planted by early sailors went wild

name: Plantain Isle
note: Plantain walks gone back to bush

name: Pineapple Cay
note: After Eleuthera's Pineapple Cays

name: Bamboo Cay
note: Bamboo clacks in the wind

name: Palmetto Cay
note: Palmetto leaves for thatch and hats

name: Lone Palm Cay
note: One palm on a hump of sand: the castaway's island of every storybook

name: Three Palms Cay
note: Three palms make a mark to steer by

name: Gulfweed Cay
note: Gulfweed: the floating sargassum that piles on its windward beach

name: Mastic Cay
note: Mastic trees; as in the Bahamas

name: Logwood Island
note: Logwood was cut for dye by the Baymen of Honduras

name: Mahogany Isle
note: Mahogany, cut for captains' cabins

name: Mast Island
note: Tall straight pines fit for masts, the most valuable timber of the age

name: Spar Island
note: Timber for yards and booms

name: Pitch Pine Island
note: Pine tar and pitch for seams and rigging

name: Cedar Isle
note: Cedar for planking light boats

name: Greenheart Island
note: Greenheart: a timber so hard the shipworm leaves it alone

name: Juniper Holm
note: Juniper scrub on a grassy holm

name: Driftwood Cay
note: Bleached driftwood stacked by the gales

name: Wrack Cay
note: Wrack: weed and wreckage cast up by the sea

name: Scrub Cay
note: Nothing but scrub; as in the Bahamas

name: Tear Coat Cay
note: A Bahamian cay whose thorny scrub tears a coat to rags

name: Turtle Grass Cay
note: Meadows of turtle grass all round it

name: Sugar Loaf Island

name: Cocked Hat Island
note: Three-cornered like a tricorne; navigators also call the triangle of three crossed bearings a cocked hat

note: Cook's name in Dusky Sound for a knob like a sailor's woollen thrum cap

name: Saddleback Island
note: Two humps and a dip like a saddle

name: Elbow Cay
note: Bent like an elbow; Abaco and the Exumas both have one

name: Table Island
note: Flat-topped and steep-sided, like Cook's Table Cape

name: Gable End Isle
note: Cook: a white cliff like the gable end of a house

name: Pigeon House Rock
note: Cook: a peak shaped like the top of a dovecote

name: Mitre Rock
note: Split at the top like a bishop's mitre

name: Steeple Rock
note: A spire of rock seen from far off

name: Chimney Stack
note: Tall, square and smoking with spray

name: Pulpit Rock
note: A ledge like a preacher's pulpit

name: Anvil Rock
note: Flat-topped with a horn at one end

name: Thimble Rock
note: Small, round and pitted

name: Kettle Rock
note: Round as a kettle, and it boils when the sea runs

name: Teapot Rock
note: A spout, a handle and a lid, if you squint

name: Coffin Island
note: Long, flat and black

name: Barrel of Butter
note: The name sailors at Scapa Flow gave a rock there

name: Plum Duff Cay
note: Duff: the sailors' boiled pudding (Smyth); a round brown lump of a cay

name: Hardtack Cay
note: Flat, dry and hard as ship's biscuit

name: Sea Pie Island

name: Burgoo Isle
note: Burgoo: seafaring porridge of boiled oatmeal (Smyth)

name: Salmagundi Cay

name: Johnny Cake Cay
note: Johnny cake: the fried bread of the islands

name: Old Wife Stack

name: Topsail Rock

name: Stranger Sail

name: Whale Rock
note: Cook's name for a sunken rock the Endeavour struck

name: Horseshoe Island
note: Curved round a lagoon

name: Sickle Cay
note: A thin curve of sand

name: Long Cay
note: The plainest and commonest cay name of all

name: Round Island
note: Plain and round

name: Flat Island
note: Cook's plainest kind of name

name: Woody Island
note: Another of Cook's plain names

name: Shipstern Cay
note: High and square at one end like a ship's stern; as in Belize

name: Capstan Isle
note: Round and drum-shaped

name: Ropewalk Island
note: Long and straight as the shed where cables are laid up

name: Monkey's Fist Rock
note: Monkey's fist: the ball knot on the end of a heaving line

name: Reef Knot Cay
note: Two loops of reef tied together

name: Bowline Island
note: Looped round a lagoon like a bowline

name: Sheepshank Cay
note: Long and doubled back on itself

name: Hawsehole Rock
note: Pierced like the hole the anchor cable runs through

name: Lubber's Hole
note: Smyth: the gap timid climbers use to get into the top; here, an arch a boat can pass

name: Needle's Eye
note: An arch too narrow for anything bigger than a jolly boat

name: Keyhole Rock
note: An arch shaped like a keyhole

name: Porthole Stack
note: A round hole through a stack

name: Bosun's Whistle
note: The wind pipes through a hole in it like a boatswain's call

name: Bellows Island
note: A blowhole breathes spray with every swell

name: Drum Rock
note: The swell booms in its cave like a drum

name: Echo Isle
note: A cave that answers back

name: Cave Holm
note: After Orkney's Helliar Holm, the cave island

name: Nobody Knows What
note: Cook's name in Dusky Sound for an arm he had no time to explore

name: Useless Island
note: A Cook name; it was

note: Cook's Luncheon Cove: where they ate lunch

name: Supper Isle
note: Cook's Supper Cove: where they ate dinner

name: Sunday Isle
note: Cook's Sunday Cove: visited on a Sunday

name: Wet Jacket Island
note: Cook's Wet Jacket Arm, where his officer was caught in a downpour

name: Turnagain Island
note: Cook's Cape Turnagain, where he met foul weather and turned back

name: Farewell Island
note: Cook's Cape Farewell, his last sight of New Zealand

name: Foulwind Isle
note: Cook's Cape Foulwind, after days of rain, squalls and gales

name: Breaksea Island
note: Cook's name for an island that shelters a sound from the swell

name: Hope Cay
note: Cook's Hope Islands, between his leaking ship and safety

note: Cook's Cape Tribulation: 'here begun all our troubles'

note: Cook's Poverty Bay 'afforded us no one thing we wanted'

note: Cook's Bay of Plenty, named to answer Poverty Bay

name: Detention Isle
note: Cook's Detention Cove

name: Occasional Cay
note: Cook's Occasional Cove

name: Runaway Cay
note: Cook's Cape Runaway

note: A Newfoundland harbour, said to have been found by sailors by chance

name: Seldom-Come-By

note: A Newfoundland harbour named in the age of sail

name: Heart's Delight

name: Heart's Desire
note: Another Newfoundland harbour name

name: Little Heart's Ease
note: A Newfoundland name: rest after a hard passage

name: Run-By-Guess
note: A Newfoundland name: found by dead reckoning and luck

name: Famish Isle
note: After Newfoundland's Famish Gut

name: Over Yonder Cay

name: Landfall Cay
note: The first land sighted after a passage

note: Charted twice, by two crews who each thought it theirs

name: Galley Packet Cay

name: Second Thoughts Cay
note: Where captains turn back

name: Fair Chance Isle
note: A fair wind and a fair chance

name: Odd Shoe Cay

note: An anchor fouled on its reef and left there

name: Broken Oar Cay
note: Half an oar stuck upright in the sand

name: Footprint Cay

name: Friday Cay

name: Sandglass Cay
note: Waisted like the glass that times the log line

name: Eight Bells Island
note: Eight bells: the end of a watch

name: Fiddler's Green

name: Cat's Paw Cay

name: Doldrum Cay
note: The doldrums: 'those parts of the sea where calms are known to prevail' (Smyth)

note: Some say the Flying Dutchman was last seen rounding it

name: Old Scratch Rock
note: Old Scratch: a sailors' name for the Devil, as Old Harry is on the Dorset stack

name: Bumbo Isle
note: Bumbo: rum, water, sugar and nutmeg

name: Rumbullion Cay

name: Kill-Devil Cay

name: Grog Blossom Isle
note: Grog-blossom: the red nose of a hard drinker (Smyth); for its red cliffs

name: Sixpence Cay
note: After the Bahamas' Six Shilling Cay, named for coins washed ashore

name: Ha'penny Rock
note: Hardly worth landing on

name: Doubloon Cay
note: A gold doubloon turned up in its sand

name: Moidore Cay
note: Moidore: the Portuguese gold coin common in the West Indies

name: Pistole Isle
note: Pistole: the Spanish gold double escudo

name: Lost Ring Cay
note: After the Exumas' Gold Ring Cay, named for something found on the beach

name: Glass Cay
note: Bahamian name for a cay strewn with glass from a wreck; or black volcanic glass

name: Bottle Cay
note: Where the current lands bottles, and the messages in them

name: Sea Chest Cay
note: A sailor's sea chest washed up here, empty

name: Silver Spoon Cay
note: Somebody's silver spoon, and no one to claim it

name: Copper-Bottom Cay
note: Copper-bottomed: sound and trustworthy, like a sheathed hull

name: Wrecker's Cay

note: Timbers from a wreck stacked above the tide line

name: Lagan Rocks
note: Lagan: goods sunk with a buoy to mark them, to be claimed later

name: Derelict Isle
note: An abandoned hull lies on its beach

name: Shroud Cay
note: Bahamian: probably for burials at sea, sewn in a shroud of sailcloth

note: Ironbound: a coast of cliffs with no landing

name: Weatherbound Island
note: Where ships wait out the wind

name: Halfway Rock
note: Halfway from port to the rim

name: Danger Cay
note: As in the Exumas, for the shoals off it

name: Mind Yourselves Rocks

name: Snoring Cay

name: Eyes-Open Rocks
note: After the Abrolhos, which sailors read as abre olhos, 'open your eyes'

name: Breakers Cay
note: Surf breaks on it in any swell

name: Grumbling Rocks
note: The surf grumbles in their gullies

name: Growler Rock
note: A low rock that growls in the swell

name: Hellweathers

name: Overfall Rock

name: Roaring Water Rocks
note: Breakers you hear long before you see them

name: Fathom Rock
note: One fathom over it at best

name: Sounding Cay
note: Where the lead goes down every few boat lengths

name: Spindrift Isle
note: Spindrift: spray blown off the crests, drifting like smoke

name: Brume Holm
note: Brume: sea mist

name: Haar Holm
note: Haar: the cold sea fog of the north

name: Spume Rock
note: Wet with flying spume in any wind

name: Loom Isle
note: Loom: 'an indistinct enlarged appearance of any distant object' (Smyth)

name: Blink Rock
note: Blink: a brightness in the sky over distant ice or land (Smyth)

note: 'Nothing further beyond': the warning said to be carved on the Pillars of Hercules

name: Hindmost Isle
note: The last island before the falls

name: Outermost Holm
note: Nothing lies beyond it but mist

name: Last Sight Cay
note: The last land a boat sees before the falls

name: Thunder Holm
note: The falls can be heard from it on a still night

note: A phantom island drawn west of Antillia in 1424

name: Mayda
note: A crescent-shaped phantom island that stayed on charts for centuries

name: Buss Island
note: Reported in 1578 near Greenland and never found again

note: Reported in 1670 in the South Atlantic; searched for and never found

note: A haunted island off Newfoundland on 16th-century maps

name: Frisland
note: A phantom island of the Zeno map

note: The drowned land of Cornish legend between Land's End and Scilly

name: Isle of Ys
note: The drowned city of Breton legend, whose bells ring under the sea

name: Thule Rock
note: Thule: the farthest land the ancients knew; ultima Thule, the end of the world

name: Fata Morgana
note: The mirage that lifts islands into the sky

name: Lodestone Island

name: Muckle Holm

name: Peerie Holm
note: Peerie: small (Shetland)

name: Outskerry
note: After the Out Skerries, the outermost rocks of Shetland

name: Auk Skerry
note: Auks nest in its cracks

name: Finfolk Skerry
note: Orkney's finfolk: sea people who row without oars

name: Trow Holm
note: Trows: the trolls of Shetland, who come out at dusk

name: Simmer Dim Isle

name: Clett Rock
note: Clett: 'a rock broken from a cliff' (Smyth)

name: The Calf

name: Holystone Island

name: Grindstone Island
note: Round, grey and gritty

name: Whetstone Rock
note: Long and grey; good for an edge

name: Millstone Rock
note: Round and flat

name: Grey Mare Rock
note: A grey hump like a horse's back

name: Clinker Island
note: Clinker: the fused lumps from a furnace; also a boat whose planks overlap

name: The Forge
note: It glows at night like a smith's forge

name: Hearth Island
note: Warm ground and steam: a hearth for cold sailors

name: Cauldron Isle
note: A crater with a boiling pool

name: Tinderbox Island
note: Dry as tinder

name: Smoky Island

name: Old Smoky
note: A peak that has been smoking as long as anyone remembers

name: Smouldering Isle
note: Its fires never quite go out

name: Pumice Cay
note: Pumice: the rock that floats

name: Burnt Island
note: A common chart name for scorched ground

name: Tumbledown Isle
note: Rubble heaped like a fallen city, as on Fallen Jerusalem in the Virgin Islands

note: Steam and sulphur where the Devil cooks

name: Furnace Island

name: Sulphur Cay

name: Greenwood Isle

name: Gloaming Isle

name: Blue Hole Cay

note: A ring of land round a lagoon like a punch bowl

note: A ring of sand round a lagoon you could stir

name: Jewel Box Isle

name: Beacon Cay

name: Watchfire Isle
note: The stones of an old watchfire on its summit

name: Old Signal Isle
note: A ruined signal station on its top

name: Chapel Cay

name: Green Flash Cay

note: The moon comes up behind it from the harbour

name: Reckoning Cay

name: Bosun's Cay
note: Where the boatswain sends the idlers to cut wood

name: Sailmaker's Isle
note: Flat ground to spread canvas on

name: Shipwright's Isle
note: Timber and a sloping beach to build on

name: Cabin Boy Cay
note: Small enough to be the cabin boy's

name: Topman's Rock
note: Only a topman could climb it

name: Purser's Cay
note: Smaller than it looks on the chart, like a purser's ration

name: Cayo Perdido
note: Spanish: the lost cay

name: Isla Sola
note: Spanish: the lonely island

name: Cayo Ciego
note: Spanish: the blind cay; low and hard to see

name: Cayo Ventoso
note: Spanish: the windy cay

name: Isla del Humo
note: Spanish: island of smoke

name: Cayo Arena
note: Spanish: sand cay; Columbus called the Ragged Islands the Islas de Arena

name: Îlet Perdu
note: French: the lost islet

name: Îlet Fortune
note: French: islet of luck; there is one off Guadeloupe

name: Îlet Brûlé
note: French: the burnt islet

name: La Désirée
note: French: the longed-for one; Columbus's men named La Désirade for the land they longed to see

name: Ilha Escondida
note: Portuguese: the hidden island

name: Broad Island
note: Bressay in Shetland is Old Norse for the broad island

name: Horse Island
note: Hrossey, the Norse name for the Orkney Mainland, means horse island

name: Grande Terre
note: French: the great land, as Guadeloupe's eastern island

name: Isla Grande
note: Spanish: the big island, a name on many Spanish charts

name: Thousand Palms Island
note: More palms than anyone has counted

name: Hollow Mountain Island
note: A broken crater with the sea let in on one side

name: Greatwood Island
note: Forest from shore to summit

name: Long Reach Island
note: Long enough to sail a reach down its whole side

name: Breakwind Island
note: It stinks of sulphur, and the wind always seems to come from it

name: Rotten Egg Cay
note: Sulphur vents; smelt long before it is seen

name: Bumboat Cay
note: Bum-boat: 'a boat employed to carry provisions, vegetables, and small merchandise for sale to ships' (Smyth); the name is from bombard, a beer vessel

name: Pooped Rock
note: Pooped: when 'a heavy sea breaks over the stern' of a boat running before a gale, 'extremely dangerous' (Smyth)

name: Seer's Rock
note: In Highland and island lore a seer had the second sight, and could foresee who would drown before the boat sailed
